=== 58000 - CTEI Comments on Proposed Transmission Allocation Rules (FINAL as filed 081126).pdf ===
                                     PROJECT NO. 58000

 RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                            §      PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL                        §               OF TEXAS
 TRANSMISSION COST RECOVERY                      §
 IN THE ERCOT REGION

                              COMMENTS OF
                CONSERVATIVE TEXANS FOR ENERGY INNOVATION

       COMES NOW Conservative Texans for Energy Innovation (CTEI) and files these

comments in response to Commission’s proposed rules approved for publication at the July 9,

2026, open meeting and filed in this proceeding on July 10, 2026. The Commission set a deadline

of August 11, 2026 for comments; therefore, these comments are timely filed.

       CTEI is a non-profit clean energy education and advocacy organization composed of

thousands of Texans seeking to promote energy innovation and clean energy policies grounded in

the conservative principle of common sense, market-based solutions that allow fair competition

and provide greater access to clean, affordable, and reliable energy.

       The principles that applied when the Commission developed transmission cost recovery

policies in the transition to competition continue to apply today. Specifically, transmission must

be built to meet peak demand and should be based on cost-causation. One of the key benefits of

the current 4CP cost allocation methodology has been encouraging loads to reduce their demand

on the grid during times of greatest demand, as peak demand traditionally has been the driver for

transmission development. Reducing the peak demand by some customers has lowered the overall

cost of the system by avoiding unnecessary transmission investment. CTEI understands the

concerns that have been raised regarding the potential for customers responding to 4CP price

signals to shift costs to residential customers, but over-correction in response to these concerns

could have the unintended consequence of harming residential customers. The more CPs that are




                                                                                                1
 included in the cost allocation methodology, the more this market signal to curtail demand when

the transmission system is stressed becomes diluted, resulting in the need to build more

transmission than otherwise would be necessary. The Commission must strike the right balance by

expanding on the current methodology while not swinging the pendulum too far in the opposite

direction. CTEI continues to prefer that the Commission make a more conservative, incremental

change by focusing its efforts on further evaluation of a 5CP or 7CP methodology, i.e., one that

captures the four summer CPs but also either a floating winter CP or CPs in December, January,

and February, the months most likely to experience extreme peak demand due to winter weather.

To the extent that the Commission chooses to adopt the 12 CP methodology, however, it should

be with the understanding that this change will dampen price signals that encourage conservation

and demand response.

       CTEI responds to the Commission’s Questions below and offers additional comments

regarding specific rule provisions.

                   COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION’S QUESTIONS

1. Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions be
   different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or different
   non-coincident (NCP) demands?

       CTEI understands the large load minimum billing demand provisions to be intended as a

protection against rapid escalation in costs for other customers on the system. While this logic is

sound, as proposed, the rules will likely have the unintended consequence of reducing a large load

customer’s incentive to reduce demand when the transmission grid is stressed. Reducing peak

demand would make existing transmission capacity available for new customers without the need

to build even more transmission capacity. Locking in a pricing structure that exacerbates the need




                                                                                                 2
 to construct more transmission capacity ultimately will cost Texans more and will also require the

taking of private property to make available additional right-of-way for those new lines.

        The proposed rules would have 100 percent of the minimum charge be based on the greater

of the large load’s contracted peak demand, the highest non-coincident peak demand on the system

in the past year, or the large load customer’s 12 CP demand. This approach fundamentally

discourages customer investment to reduce demand on the grid, either by installing on-site

generation or through demand response to reduce stress on the grid during periods of peak demand.

CTEI recommends that the Commission modify this concept to more of a hybrid approach, as

discussed below.

        To be clear, CTEI supports requiring large loads to have more “skin in the game” for

proposed interconnections and to ensure that all large load customers contribute equitably for the

cost of the transmission grid they and all other Texans rely on for reliable electric service. CTEI

supports requiring large load customers to pay a minimum billing demand charge over a period of

time based on the large load customer’s contracted demand. At the same time, the Commission’s

cost allocation policy going forward should continue to provide incentives for loads to reduce the

burden on the grid, especially during times of stress – a benefit of the 4CP methodology, and, to a

lesser extent the 12CP methodology. Under this hybrid approach, CTEI recommends that the

Commission consider modifying the minimum billing demand charge to be a maximum of 75

percent fixed, based on the customer’s contracted peak demand, with the remaining 25 percent of

the customer’s demand charge being based on 12CP. CTEI appreciates the research the Texas

Energy Buyers Alliance (TEBA) submitted in this proceeding to calculate the appropriate duration

of a minimum charge based on the magnitude of the minimum charge.1 Based on their study, a



1
    Comments of the Texas Energy Buyers Alliance, July 30, 2026.


                                                                                                 3
 minimum demand charge of 75 percent should remain in effect for approximately 13 years to

ensure existing customers are held harmless.2 During this period, the remaining 25 percent of the

customer demand charge would be based on demand based on 12 CP. This 25 percent charge

would still encourage a customer to reduce peak demand through demand response or through

installation of some on-site generation, thereby making more peak demand capacity available to

other customers.

2. Should the large load minimum billing demand be:
   a. fixed for 20 years as proposed;
   b. reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or
   c. extended to a longer time period?

         Fixing the large load minimum billing demand charge for 20 years as proposed would be

excessive. As noted above, TEBA has provided analytical support for a shorter duration of a

minimum billing demand. CTEI recognizes that there is a balance to be struck regarding ensuring

that large loads pay for transmission resources that are built to meet their needs based on their

representations regarding their expected demand on the grid. At the same time, minimum demand

charges may have the unintended consequence of discouraging large loads from investing in on-

site generation in the future that can reduce a load’s demand on the grid and support increased

reliable operations of the ERCOT System or developing demand response capabilities that will

benefit all customers.

3. Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of demand
   lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example, should the large
   load minimum billing demand:
   a. reflect a “ratcheted” demand, wherein the large load minimum billing demand is
      some percentage of the customer’s contracted peak demand or maximum NCP
      demand in the previous year? If so, should the ratchet percentage decline in phases
      over the years, and how?
   b. be based on a “weighted average” minimum billing demand, wherein the large load
      minimum billing demand is some weighted average of the large load customer’s
      contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand over the previous year and the large
2
    Id. at 7.


                                                                                               4
        load customer’s 12CP demand? If so, should the percentage weighting towards
       contracted peak demand or NCP demand decline in phases over the years, and how?
       See CTEI’s response to Question No. 1. A portion of the minimum charge should be fixed,

and the remaining portion should be based on 12CP so that the customer has the incentive to find

ways to use the system more efficiently.

   Further, reliance on NCP demand charges discourages customers from shifting demand from

peak periods to times of lower stress on the grid. In addition, the sum of all customers’ NCPs can

be greater than the actual peak demand on the grid. This result increases the potential that a

transmission utility will over-recover its actual costs.

4. Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load, defined as an
   entity that is subject to §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection
   Standards) and in which 50% or greater of the demand at the site consists of power
   electronic based load, specifically computational load, such as data centers and
   cryptocurrency mining facilities? Responses to this question should include applicable
   legal support or limitations regarding separate rate treatment for large computational
   loads.

       No response.

5. Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include
   transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to serve
   the transmission capacity needs of a particular load?

       No. Interconnection costs are billed to a customer and not included in a utility’s rate base

because these facilities are solely used by the customer for their benefit. In contrast, the

transmission system improvements that are identified through the Batch Study Process will

ultimately benefit all customers on the ERCOT System through a more stable and reliable system.

The transmission cost allocation methodology should reflect the broader benefit of these

investments.

6. If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of whether
   the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity, how should
   these loads be reflected in the resource adequacy reports and assessments and
   transmission planning studies?



                                                                                                 5
         Including a reservation process raises numerous questions regarding the various load

scenarios that would be used to evaluate the need for any potential element of the transmission

grid, which in turn raises questions about which loads get prioritized for service and which loads

are relegated to a lower priority. The reservation process would be opening a whole Pandora’s

Box, with impacts on all of the associated reports, assessments, and studies upon which ERCOT,

the Commission, market participants, and the public rely for accurate grid information, and CTEI

is concerned about the consequences of this approach.

        ERCOT should be allowed to consider load ramp schedules to determine what transmission

capacity that is available today is expected to be used in the future. When capacity is not expected

to be used, ERCOT should be able to take that available capacity into account as it plans the

gradual expansion of the grid. This strategy would avoid over-investment in capacity in the near

term.

        Through the Batch Study Process, ERCOT will allocate load ramping capability to loads

that are studied and allocated. To the extent that transmission capability becomes available faster

than the ERCOT-determined load ramp, the customer should either be allowed to increase its load

ramp to match the cost allocation of the transmission capacity, or the cost allocation should be

reduced.

        Finally, a transmission capacity reservation process should not be conflated to equal a

generation capacity reservation process that impacts resource adequacy reports.          While the

reservation of transmission can be an indicator of future demand growth, these are not

synonymous.




                                                                                                  6
                    COMMENTS ON SPECIFIC PROPOSED RULE LANGUAGE

§25.192 Transmission Service Rates.

       §25.192(c) Tariffs.

       CTEI supports the Commission’s proposed requirement in subsection (c)(2) that a utility

timely file a tariff to provide transmission service at distribution voltage. CTEI also recommends

that the Commission develop a uniform interconnection agreement for these customers as it

considers developing a standard tariff for transmission service at transmission voltage.

       §25.192(f) Billing units.

       This subsection establishes the 12CP methodology. Regarding paragraph (f)(1)(B), and

specifically the last sentence, if a customer is not allowed to fully use the available capacity

because of limitations in an ERCOT-mandated load commissioning plan (LCP), ERCOT should

allow the customer to accelerate its LCP so that it can utilize the available capacity or else the

customer should not be required to pay for capacity that it is prohibited from accessing.

       §25.192(k) Large load customer interconnection fee and financial security.

       In paragraph (k)(2), relating to financial security, the Commission should provide guidance

regarding the period over which the forfeited financial security will be amortized. A quick

application of these funds can lead to near term rate reduction, but longer-term rate shock when

the initial benefit of the application of the funds passes.

§25.193 Distribution Service Provider Transmission Cost Recovery Factor (TCRF).

       §25.193(d) Large load minimum billing demand

       As discussed above in CTEI’s response to Question No. 1, requiring the minimum billing

demand to be the greater of the amounts specified in paragraphs (d)(2)(A), (B), or (C) will




                                                                                                7
 discourage efficient use of the transmission grid and investments to reduce stress on the grid in

times of peak demand through demand response or investment in on-site generation.

       Regarding paragraph (d)(3), as noted above in response to Question No. 2, a minimum

charge for 20 years is too long. TEBA’s study provides support for a shorter time period for the

minimum charge. In addition, a customer should not be required to pay for capacity that an

ERCOT-imposed LCP prohibits the customer from being able to access.

       §25.193(e) Adjustments due to delayed cost recovery or billing information.

       CTEI appreciates the need to allow these mechanisms for adjustments, but the resulting

rates should remain cost-based and not be made for the purpose of cross-subsidization.

§25.252, Large Load Customer Tariffs

       §25.252(c) TSP and IOU-DSP tariff requirements

       Regarding the contribution in aid to construction (CIAC) provision in (c)(2)(ii), CTEI

recommends that the manner in which CIAC must be paid should be consistent with the

Commission-approved amendments to Planning Guide Section 9.2.1.1(1)(f)(vii), i.e., allowing

CIAC to be satisfied either by direct cash payment or by posting financial security.

       §25.252(d) TSP Tariff Requirements

       Subsection (d)(1) establishes requirements for a large load customer to reserve

transmission capacity. As discussed in our response to Question No. 6, CTEI is concerned about

modifying policy to reserve transmission capacity. Such policy would be a radical departure from

the existing postage stamp policy that has served ERCOT so well. The postage stamp transmission

policy is one of the most fundamental building blocks that has been in place since ERCOT’s

transition to competition and has been a fundamental reason why generation resources have been

better able to locate in the ERCOT region than other parts of the United States and customers have




                                                                                                8
 been able to locate in the ERCOT Region without concern that they may shoulder much higher

transmission costs than non-ERCOT parts of the state.

       To the extent that the Commission adopts a policy change to allow for capacity

reservations, then if a large load customer is allowed to reserve capacity, then they should pay for

it accordingly. Further, ERCOT should be able to allocate capacity that is not yet used to meet

near-term needs on the grid to support a more manageable expansion schedule for the grid.

       Regarding the reallocation provision in paragraph (d)(2), and due to the cross reference in

subparagraph §25.252(d)(1)(D) to an as-yet unadopted rule §25.194, relating to Large Load

Interconnection Standards, it is not yet completely clear regarding all possible instances in which

transmission capacity may be reallocated. CTEI recommends that all potential scenarios for

reallocation should be addressed in the same rule rather than separately addressed in two or more

rules. Separating provisions into multiple rules will only create confusion, not clarity.

       §25.252(e) IOU-DSP tariff requirements.

       Regarding subparagraph (e)(2)(i), and as discussed previously regarding §25.192(f)(1)(b),

Commission rules should take into account that the delay in the use of available capacity could be

due to an ERCOT-mandated LCP. Therefore, an LCP should be allowed to be accelerated to

address when transmission capacity ultimately becomes available, or financial liability for the

capacity should be delayed until the LCP itself is not a limiting factor.

       Regarding subparagraph (e)(2)(ii), we reiterate our comments regarding paragraph

§25.193(d) above. Also, regarding (e)(2)(ii)(B), this should be clarified that a higher charge is

applied prospectively; in other words, not all 240 payments must be adjusted if there is a higher

NCP in a later year. For example, a higher NCP in year 5 should not require an adjustment to

payments previously made in years 1-4.




                                                                                                  9
                                         CONCLUSION

         CTEI appreciates the opportunity to submit comments regarding transmission cost

recovery in ERCOT and encourages the Commission to adopt policies that fairly allocate costs

based on cost-causation principles, ensure appropriately broad-based cost recovery of investments

in the transmission grid, and promote infrastructure development and economic prosperity in the

state.

                                            Respectfully submitted,

                                             /s/ Matt Welch

ultimately benefit all customers on the ERCOT System through a more stable and reliable system.

The transmission cost allocation methodology should reflect the broader benefit of these

investments.

6. If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of whether
    the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity, how should
    these loads be rellected in the resource adequacy reports and assessments and
    transmission planning studies?



                                                                                                 5
         Including a reservation process raises numerous questions regarding the various load

scenarios that would be used to evaluate the need for any potential element of the transmission

grid, which in turn raises questions about which loads get prioritized for service and which loads

are relegated to a lower priority. The reservation process would be opening a whole Pandora' s

Box, with impacts on all of the associated reports, assessments, and studies upon which ERCOT,

the Commission, market participants, and the public rely for accurate grid information, and CTEI

is concerned about the consequences of this approach.

        ERCOT should be allowed to consider load ramp schedules to determine what transmission

capacity that is available today is expected to be used in the future. When capacity is not expected

to be used, ERCOT should be able to take that available capacity into account as it plans the

gradual expansion of the grid. This strategy would avoid over-investment in capacity in the near

term.
        Through the Batch Study Process, ERCOT will allocate load ramping capability to loads

that are studied and allocated. To the extent that transmission capability becomes available faster

than the ERCOT-determined load ramp, the customer should either be allowed to increase its load

ramp to match the cost allocation of the transmission capacity, or the cost allocation should be

reduced.
        Finally, a transmission capacity reservation process should not be conflated to equal a

generation capacity reservation process that impacts resource adequacy reports.          While the

reservation of transmission can be an indicator of future demand growth, these are not

synonymous.




                                                                                                  6
                    COMMENTS ON SPECIFIC PROPOSED RULE LANGUAGE

§25.192 Transmission Service Rates.

        §25.192(c) Tariffs.

        CTEI supports the Commission' s proposed requirement in subsection (c)(2) that a utility

timely file a tariff to provide transmission service at distribution voltage. CTEI also recommends

that the Commission develop a uniform interconnection agreement for these customers as it

considers developing a standard tariff for transmission service at transmission voltage.

        §25.1920 Billing units.

        This subsection establishes the 12CP methodology. Regarding paragraph (f)(1)(B), and

specifically the last sentence, if a customer is not allowed to fully use the available capacity

because of limitations in an ERCOT-mandated load commissioning plan (LCP), ERCOT should

allow the customer to accelerate its LCP so that it can utilize the available capacity or else the

customer should not be required to pay for capacity that it is prohibited from accessing.

        §25.192(k) Large load customer interconnection fee andjinancial security.

        In paragraph (k)(2), relating to financial security, the Commission should provide guidance

regarding the period over which the forfeited financial security will be amortized. A quick

application of these funds can lead to near term rate reduction, but longer-term rate shock when

the initial benefit of the application of the funds passes.

§25.193 Distribution Service Provider Transmission Cost Recovery Factor (TCRF).

        §25.193(d) Large load minimum billing demand

        As discussed above in CTEI's response to Question No. 1, requiring the minimum billing

demand to be the greater of the amounts specified in paragraphs (d)(2)(A), (B), or (C) will




                                                                                                 7
 discourage efficient use of the transmission grid and investments to reduce stress on the grid in

times of peak demand through demand response or investment in on-site generation.

       Regarding paragraph (d)(3), as noted above in response to Question No. 2, a minimum

charge for 20 years is too long. TEBA's study provides support for a shorter time period for the

minimum charge. In addition, a customer should not be required to pay for capacity that an

ERCOT-imposed LCP prohibits the customer from being able to access.

       §25.193(e) Adjustments due to delayed cost recovery or billing information.

       CTEI appreciates the need to allow these mechanisms for adjustments, but the resulting

rates should remain cost-based and not be made for the purpose of cross-subsidization.

§25.252, Large Load Customer Tariffs

       §25.252(c) TSPand IOU-DSP tariff requirements

       Regarding the contribution in aid to construction (CIAC) provision in (c)(2)(ii), CTEI

recommends that the manner in which CIAC must be paid should be consistent with the

Commission-approved amendments to Planning Guide Section 9.2.1.1(1)(f)(vii), i.e., allowing

CIAC to be satisfied either by direct cash payment or by posting financial security.

       §25.252(d) TSPTariff Requirements

       Subsection (d)(1) establishes requirements for a large load customer to reserve

transmission capacity. As discussed in our response to Question No. 6, CTEI is concerned about

modifying policy to reserve transmission capacity. Such policy would be a radical departure from

the existing postage stamp policy that has served ERCOT so well. The postage stamp transmission

policy is one of the most fundamental building blocks that has been in place since ERCOT's

transition to competition and has been a fundamental reason why generation resources have been

better able to locate in the ERCOT region than other parts of the United States and customers have
 been able to locate in the ERCOT Region without concern that they may shoulder much higher

transmission costs than non-ERCOT parts of the state.

       To the extent that the Commission adopts a policy change to allow for capacity

reservations, then if a large load customer is allowed to reserve capacity, then they should pay for

it accordingly. Further, ERCOT should be able to allocate capacity that is not yet used to meet

near-term needs on the grid to support a more manageable expansion schedule for the grid.

       Regarding the reallocation provision in paragraph (d)(2), and due to the cross reference in

subparagraph §25.252(d)(1)(D) to an as-yet unadopted rule §25.194, relating to Large Load

Interconnection Standards, it is not yet completely clear regarding all possible instances in which

transmission capacity may be reallocated. CTEI recommends that all potential scenarios for

reallocation should be addressed in the same rule rather than separately addressed in two or more

rules. Separating provisions into multiple rules will only create confusion, not clarity.

       §25.252(e) IOU-DSP tariffrequirements.

       Regarding subparagraph (e)(2)(i), and as discussed previously regarding §25.192(f)(1)(b),

Commission rules should take into account that the delay in the use of available capacity could be

due to an ERCOT-mandated LCP. Therefore, an LCP should be allowed to be accelerated to

address when transmission capacity ultimately becomes available, or financial liability for the

capacity should be delayed until the LCP itself is not a limiting factor.

       Regarding subparagraph (e)(2)(ii), we reiterate our comments regarding paragraph

§25.193(d) above. Also, regarding (e)(2)(ii)(B), this should be clarified that a higher charge is

applied prospectively; in other words, not all 240 payments must be adjusted if there is a higher

NCP in a later year. For example, a higher NCP in year 5 should not require an adjustment to

payments previously made in years 1-4.
